record_identity.title: AI-hallucinated references entered Australian parliamentary inquiry submissions

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Australian parliamentary inquiry submissions containing apparent AI-hallucinated references
incident_identity.date_basis: 1 September 2026 is used as the public-reporting date of Guardian Australia's investigation. The affected submissions span inquiries in the current Australian parliament and were created before that report; this record does not assert 1 September as the first occurrence.

summary: Guardian Australia reported identifying at least 39 submissions to Australian parliamentary and political inquiries containing apparent hallucinated references, including invented sources, incorrect citations and misstatements of real research. In some cases, parliamentary committee reports cited submissions in which many cited sources appeared not to exist. The reporting also described instances in which AI search systems subsequently surfaced or summarised the false references, increasing the difficulty of later verification.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Guardian Australia reports that it extracted references from current-parliament inquiry submissions, checked them against Crossref, Google Scholar and DOI resolution, manually reviewed documents with high unmatched-reference rates, and identified at least 39 submissions containing what appeared to be hallucinated references. The report documents examples of nonexistent papers attributed to real academics, misstatement of real research, and committee reports citing affected submissions. A later News24 item described continuing concern about policy submissions containing AI hallucinations entering parliament and carried commentary that submitters remain accountable for AI-generated work.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The occurrence is a high-reliance epistemic-integrity failure: generated or AI-assisted claims and citations that may appear plausible at draft level were submitted into parliamentary evidence channels without satisfying the factual, source and evidentiary fidelity required for institutional policy reliance. The failure is not simply that generative systems can produce incorrect text; it is the promotion of insufficiently verified symbolic content into a formal evidence-bearing context.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: For CAM, the occurrence directly instantiates Annex L's distinction between low-reliance exploratory generation and public or structural reliance. Parliamentary submissions can shape inquiry records, committee reasoning and policy development, so epistemic posture must scale with that downstream reliance. The case also shows how false references can become recursively reinforced when search and AI systems later cite the contaminated submission itself.
assessment_boundaries: Guardian Australia's detection method identifies unmatched or incorrect references and then applies manual review; it is not a definitive detector of AI authorship for every affected submission.
The record does not assert that every incorrect citation was produced by an LLM or that every affected submission materially changed a parliamentary decision.
The Guardian reports that some authors acknowledged AI use or AI-assisted research, while others attributed errors to human process failures or were unaware of AI limitations.

The News24 video page was discoverable through current search indexing, but direct page retrieval returned an error in the review environment; only the indexed title and short description are relied upon here.
This Incident records contamination of a parliamentary evidence channel and associated reliance risk; it does not determine misconduct, liability or sanctions for individual submitters.

severity_assessment.materialised_consequence: At least 39 parliamentary or political inquiry submissions were reported to contain apparent hallucinated references, including nonexistent sources and incorrect attribution of real research; some affected submissions were subsequently cited in parliamentary committee reports.
severity_assessment.affected_scope: The evidenced scope spans multiple Australian parliamentary and political inquiries in the current parliament, affected submission authors, committees, researchers whose work was misattributed, and downstream readers of committee material. The report does not establish that every inquiry or policy outcome was affected.
severity_assessment.seriousness_and_persistence: The occurrence produced meaningful institutional information-integrity harm and contamination of evidence-bearing records, with potential persistence because published submissions and committee reports can remain searchable and can be re-ingested by search or AI systems. The evidence does not establish a specific grave policy outcome, irreversible rights deprivation, or comparably severe realised harm.
severity_assessment.quantitative_information: Guardian Australia reports at least 39 submissions containing apparent hallucinated references and more than 100 papers containing ChatGPT URL tags. It states that some submissions had only a few incorrect citations while others contained references where every cited source appeared not to exist. The total number of affected parliamentary decisions is not established.
severity_assessment.evidentiary_limits: The investigation method is conservative but not a universal AI detector; incorrect references do not prove AI use in every case. The record does not establish the full causal effect on committee findings, legislation or government policy.
severity_assessment.band_rationale: S3 rather than S2 is appropriate because the evidence establishes meaningful and recurring contamination of a democratic evidence process but does not identify a specific substantial policy, rights, financial or operational harm at the S2 level. S3 rather than S4 is appropriate because the issue affected dozens of submissions, entered formal committee-report pathways and can persist through recursive search and citation, exceeding a local or readily remediable presentation error.
